newsitem.title: THAILAND: Clinton in Thailand, final stop on Asian tour.
newsitem.headline: Clinton in Thailand, final stop on Asian tour.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton arrived in Thailand on Monday night for a 27-hour visit to the booming southeast Asian kingdom, a key ally and magnet for U.S. trade and investment.

Clinton, the first U.S. leader to visit the kingdom since Richard Nixon in 1969, received a low-key ceremonial welcome at Don Muang International Airport where he was joined by his wife Hillary after her separate trip to northern Thailand.

The Clintons then went to Chitrlada Palace, a sprawling estate known for its colourful gardens and stable of white elephants, for a late-night audience with King Bhumibol and his consort, Queen Sirikit.

"I've read a lot about him. He's been a very constructive influence in his country, and he loves jazz music," Clinton told reporters on Air Force One during the flight to Bangkok, the last stop of a 12-day post-election trip to Hawaii, Australia and Asia.

The president seemed awed by his surroundings in the opulent palace, with its peaked Oriental roofs festooned with brightly-coloured lights. "I was with the Sultan of Brunei today. He sends his regards," Clinton said as he greeted Bhumibol.

A senior U.S. official said Clinton's visit was arranged to help the U.S.-born monarch mark his 50th anniversary on the Thai throne. "There's no big negotiation or tough issue. He's just showing U.S. support for a friendly ally," the official said.
The highlight of Clinton's overnight visit was to be a speech on Tuesday at Chulalongkorn University. He was also to witness the signing of a U.S.-Thai tax treaty.
The treaty, which took more than a decade of negotiations, ends double taxation with the aim of encouraging investment and technology transfer.
Two-way trade amounts to about $18 billion a year. Thailand is the U.S.'s 18th largest trading partner, and it also hosts the largest U.S. military exercise in Asia, Operation Cobra Gold.

Earlier on Monday, Clinton took part in the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the Philippine port of Subic Bay and came away with a big policy victory -- APEC's endorsement of a U.S. push for a global free trade agreement on computers and telecommunications equipment.
Such an agreement "should substantially eliminate tariffs by the year 2000," leaders of the 18 APEC economies said in a summit communique.l
Clinton, talking to officials of the U.S. embassy in Manila, called APEC's action "a big deal" that would contribute to U.S. economic growth.

"Every year, we sell $100 billion in information technology and that sector supports almost two million jobs in the United States. So imagine if we went to zero tariffs in the entire world what that would mean to America for exports and higher paying jobs," he said.

Clinton planned to discuss economic and security issues with Thai officials as well as efforts to eradicate the drug trade and trafficking still rampant in the so-called Golden Triangle region. Retired U.S. Army Gen. Barry McCaffrey, the director of U.S. drug cvontrol policy, was to take part in the talks, U.S. officials said.
